newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban calls U.N. conference useless.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban calls U.N. conference useless.

text.p: Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban movement dismissed as useless on Monday a conference convened by the United Nations to discuss the war-torn country's problems without anybody representing it.
The U.N. meeting on Afghanistan in New York later on Monday is the latest in a series of attempts to persuade warring Afghan factions to negotiate a peaceful end to the conflict.
But the Taleban, which rules most of the country and controls the capital Kabul, said the conference was contrary to the Afghan people's wishes.

"Any conference, meeting...regarding Afghanistan without Afghanistan's representatives is a useless action," said a commentary by the official Bakhtar news agency broadcast by the Taleban-controlled Kabul Radio.
The broadcast, monitored in Islamabad, quoted the agency as saying the United Nations should have recognised the Taleban government if it were serious about the Afghan problem.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul in late September and now controls almost 75 percent of the country, claims Afghanistan's seat in the U.N., currently occupied by a representative of the ousted government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
None of the invited countries has admitted backing any of the factions since the fall of the communist regime in 1992, and all warring parties insist they are not receiving outside aid.

Representatives of countries thought to be able to exert influence over the parties in the Afghan war were gathering in New York on Monday at the invitation of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
According to a U.N. officer in Kabul, the aim is "to see if the participating countries can decide among themselves on ways of harnessing their influence in support of peace".

Countries invited to the New York meeting include the five permanent members of the U.N. Security Souncil -- the United States, Britain, Russia, France and China -- as well as Afghanistan's neighbours and others.

They include Pakistan, Iran, India, Uzbekistan and Saudi Arabia, all of them accused by each other and by Afghan factions of contributing to the conflagration at one time or another. The warring factions have not been invited.
"If the United Nations wants to bring peace to the country, it should have pressurised India, Russia and Iran against interfering in Afghan affairs," the Bakhtar commentary said.

Rabbani's government accused Pakistan of aiding Taleban, a charge denied by Islamabad, which says it has no favourites among the Afghan factions, most of whom it helped during their guerrilla war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.

"The convening of the U.N. conference on Afghanistan is against the wishes of the Afghan people because there are same noodles in the same bowl," the Bakhtar commentary said. "People expect nothing positive or agreeable from the conference."
Afghan watchers in Kabul said foreign interference was rampant and would be almost impossible to stop.
"Foreign interference is a fact of life in Afghanistan, and the U.N. will have to learn to live with it," said one.
The first objective of the meeting in New York will be to forge a consensus among the participants on a plan that safeguards their strategic concerns.

Given the long-standing divisions between the surrounding states, Monday's one-day meeting is unlikely to result in a concrete plan of action, but it might produce a framework for co-operation in the future.
The meeting is also a sign that the world's powers, after four years of neglect, are finally taking a serious interest in ending the carnage in Afghanistan.
